title: Reading pricing tables and attributing usage

opening.headline: To explain where the numbers on your bill come from, you need to be able to read price lists and attribute usage to teams and projects.
body: Let's say your AI API bill arrives at the end of the month, but you only see the amount and no idea which team used which feature. The finance team asks why it is higher than last month, and the development team cannot provide any justification other than the number of response tokens. This is because if the same account and key are shared by multiple teams, the costs are lumped together.

In this class, we will look at how token charging is calculated as the product of unit price and usage, and how the three companies' price structures are similar and different. We then distinguish between cost attribution methods through APIs for querying usage and costs, workspaces, FinOps allocation, and multi-tenant metering.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the three companies' pricing structure and usage/cost API
Cost attribution methods can be distinguished by team and project.

paragraphs: At the end of the month, the AI API bill arrived. The amount has increased significantly since last month, but the invoice only shows the total and does not indicate which function and which team spent how much.

The finance team asks why it is higher than last month. The development team has no justification other than the fact that the number of response tokens has increased. This is because it is not clear whether the input token has increased, the output token has increased, the cache has been broken, or which model the increase has occurred in.

A bigger problem is when multiple teams share the same account and key. Costs are lumped together, and since no one knows their share, there is no incentive to cut back. The question for this lesson is what unit price multiplied by usage is the billing amount and whose share will be divided?

callout.label: Things to think about

screens.outro: First, let me recall a moment in my experience when it was difficult to split costs.

screens.title: Remember: Whose Cost Is It?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced difficulty splitting costs due to multiple services being called with a shared API key?
items.answer: If multiple services use one key, the usage is combined into one line and cannot be distinguished by service. If you want to share it later, you have to go through the call records one by one. It is much easier to split keys and bundles by service or team from the beginning.

items.prompt: The month my bill suddenly went up, how long did it take to find the cause?
items.answer: The time it takes to find the cause depends on what units you can view the usage in. If you can search by model, day, key, and workspace, it only takes a few minutes, but if you only have the total, it may take several days.

items.prompt: Have you ever wanted to split costs by project or environment?
items.answer: This is the most common need when development and operational environments and multiple projects are within the same organization. The structures that meet this need are workspace and cost attribution. In this lesson, we'll look at specific methods.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's start by reading the price list to see how the costs are calculated.

screens.title: Token charging and price list read
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: AI API cost is calculated by multiplying the quantities of input and output tokens by their respective unit prices and adding the results. Prices are usually quoted per million tokens. Output tokens generally cost more than input tokens. Cached input uses a separate cache-read rate; tokens written to the cache use a cache-write rate. Some models vary their prices by prompt-length tier, and conditions such as data residency may introduce a multiplier. Agent Platform states that input and output charges apply only to requests returning an HTTP 200 response. When reading a price list, therefore, check input, output, cache-read, cache-write, and multiplier charges, not just one unit price.

terms.tip: There are two basic usages for calculating costs: Each has a different unit price, and even if the same token increases, the cost increase varies depending on which side increases.
A common unit of expression in price lists. The actual cost of one request is estimated by dividing the number of tokens by 1 million and multiplying it by the unit price.
The unit price applied to input tokens read from the cache. It is priced lower than the regular input unit price, reducing the cost of repeated prefixes.
This is the unit price applied to each new token written to the cache. If it's never read, writing costs can only increase.
This is the multiplier that is multiplied by the basic unit price. It can be attached to conditions such as data residence or fast mode, and if multiple conditions overlap, they are stacked.

data.notes: Because the absolute value of a unit price changes, it is important to learn how to read the structure rather than just memorize the numbers. The structure is organized into five elements: input, output, cache reads and writes, discount, and multiplier. Even if you come across a new price list, you can calculate costs in the same way as long as you find items that fit into these five elements.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to read the structure, let's see how to look up usage and costs in code.

screens.title: Usage & Cost API and SDK cost tracking
screens.lead: Read the request below to see how to view your usage and costs. The explanation on the right also lists symptoms when search conditions are specified incorrectly.

data.code:
#Usage per day, by model
curl "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/organizations/usage_report/messages?\
starting_at=2025-01-01T00:00:00Z&\
ending_at=2025-01-08T00:00:00Z&\
group_by%5B%5D=model&\
bucket_width=1d" \
  -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \
  -H "x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_ADMIN_KEY"

#Cost per workspace (USD)
curl "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/organizations/cost_report?\
starting_at=2025-01-01T00:00:00Z&\
ending_at=2025-01-31T00:00:00Z&\
group_by%5B%5D=workspace_id&\
group_by%5B%5D=description" \
  -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \
  -H "x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_ADMIN_KEY"

notes.note: The Usage and Cost Admin API programmatically queries an organization's past usage and costs for accurate token counting and billing comparison. usage_report/messages returns token usage, with a period defined by starting_at and ending_at. If you do not specify a period or set it too broadly, it will be difficult to find the desired section.

Bucket_width groups usage into 1 minute, 1 hour, and 1 day sections, and group_by groups it by model, workspace, service tier, etc. You can also filter by API key or workspace. If group_by is omitted, only the sum is returned and you cannot tell where the increase occurred.

You will need an Admin API key. It is not called with a regular API key; Claude Enterprise uses a separate Analytics API key. Management keys can read information across the entire organization, so be careful about storing them.

cost_report returns the cost of the service level in USD. When you group by workspace, you get costs by team or project. For usage and costs attributed to the default workspace, the workspace_id is null.

The total_cost_usd in Claude Agent SDK is an estimate calculated from local price lists and may differ from your actual billing. Confirmation is based on billing data. By integrating with observation platforms such as Datadog or Grafana Cloud, you can also create dashboards and notifications without code.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to look up, let’s look at the structure of attributing costs to teams and projects.

screens.title: Cost and FinOps allocation by workspace
screens.lead: When you select each item, an explanation of the structure for attributing costs to teams and projects will appear. Open them all and think about what kind of structure your organization needs.

items.title: Claude Workspace
items.body: Workspace divides usage by project, environment, and team while billing and management are done in one place. API keys can be limited to workspaces, and each workspace can have member and resource limits. When you group by workspace in the usage inquiry, the cost by team is immediately displayed.

items.title: Claude Code's per-user limits
items.body: Claude Code creates per-user keys in a separate workspace and supports per-user monthly spending limits only in this workspace. This means that if you want to set a limit on an individual basis, you must configure a separate workspace accordingly.

items.title: The three pillars of FinOps allocation
items.body: The FinOps Framework describes allocation as the ability to determine how costs will be divided and attributed to those responsible for each component. Metadata such as account structure, tags, and labels identify which category a cost falls into. There are three strategies to achieve this: An allocation strategy determines how the organization wants to view costs, for example, by cost center for finance or by application for engineering. Tagging and hierarchy strategies establish rules for mapping usage and resources to their units: tags, naming standards, and account bundles. A shared cost strategy determines how shared costs will be divided among multiple parties.

items.title: Showback and chargeback
items.body: In the FinOps Framework, showbacks are a way to show each group the costs of their scope but not reflect them in the accounting budget. We view this as a basic activity required for all FinOps practices. Chargeback is a more formal way of allocating the same cost to an organization's official accounting budget through the financial system, and whether it is necessary depends on the organization's accounting policies. Neither one is more mature. Both are possible only if there is an allocation first. It is desirable to institutionalize ownership information so that it is required at the time of resource creation, because organizing tags later is already an ownerless cost.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the attribution structure, let's look at the metering problem in shared resources.

ext.title: FinOps Foundation, FinOps Framework: Invoicing & Chargeback

screens.title: Shared responsibility model and multi-tenant metering
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the structure in which the platform weighs and the structure in which you have to meter yourself.

states.label: When the platform distinguishes
states.body: Platforms that tabulate usage records, such as Databricks' Billable Usage System Table, can analyze the records to break down costs. Even in cases where the structure itself divides usage, such as Claude Workspace, attribution is made only through inquiries. In this case, the customer's work is focused on how to design the division units.

states.label: When you need to weigh yourself
states.body: There are three models for configuring resources in multi-tenant services: In the terminology of AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens, silo is a method of having dedicated resources for each tenant, pool is a method of sharing resources such as compute and storage by tenants, and bridge is a method of mixing some into silos and some into pools depending on the components. Pools have the advantage of economies of scale and convenience of management, but metering becomes more important because usage is not automatically divided by tenant. Most shared services do not automatically classify usage by tenant, so providers must measure it themselves. Determine representative metrics, such as storage capacity or key transaction counts, and occasionally check your assumptions against actual consumption. If one tenant monopolizes resources, a noisy neighbor problem occurs where other tenants fail. The Claude App Gateway natively calls into one shared upstream entitlement, so your provider bill is not split per developer, and you can set per-developer daily, weekly, and monthly spending limits. The first step is to find out how much the platform gives out.

screens.outro: Now that you've seen the concepts, let's step through a real-life tracking example.

ext.title: AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens, Silo, Pool, and Bridge Models

screens.title: Illustrative Case: Tracking Back a Claim
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: This month's expenses have increased significantly compared to last month. The finance team is asking the cause, and the development team must explain within today. A totals-only report can't explain things, so it tracks broadly and narrowly.

steps.title: Step 1: Find out where the increase occurred
steps.body: Use the Usage API to group usage by day and model to find which model has increased on which day. If the usage of a certain model has increased after a certain date, it can be a clue to check the distribution or change at that time.

steps.title: Step 2: Multiply and compare with unit price
steps.body: Input, output, cache read and write tokens are multiplied by each unit price and matched against billing. If the multiplied value doesn't match your bill, check to see if there is a missing multiplier or unit price range. At this stage it is revealed which type of token is driving up the cost.

steps.title: Step 3: Re-divide into workspaces
steps.body: Divide further by workspace to see output token growth for specific projects. If the increase is concentrated in one project, the cause is a change in that project. If the increase is evenly spread, it is a common factor such as unit cost or model configuration.

steps.title: Step 4: Take action and determine the cause
steps.body: If the cause is a cache miss for a long prompt, fix the prefix. Do not check the result of the action using total_cost_usd, which is an estimate from the SDK, but confirm it with billing data. This is because estimates are calculated from local price lists and may differ from actual charges.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: In this case, the tracking took just a few minutes because we were able to break usage down into models, days, and workspaces. If it were a structure that couldn't be divided, the same tracking would have taken several days.

screens.outro: Now that we've tracked it down, let's summarize why attribution is necessary.

screens.title: Explanatory Case Study: Why Attribution of Usage to Departments is Necessary
screens.lead: As you select each item, the difference before and after attribution and the reasons for it will unfold. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.answer: All departments use one key, so only the total amount is visible and no one knows which department raised it. Even if there is talk of cutting costs, no one feels like it is their job.

Divide costs by departmental workspaces, keys, and tags, and each person sees their share. Monthly changes can also be explained by department, allowing you to immediately answer questions from the finance team.

items.prompt: Why do costs go down when liability is seen?
items.answer: Visible accountability creates incentives for budgets, limits, and optimization. This gives you reason to use savings like caching and batching. This is how the FinOps principle works: everyone is responsible for their own usage.

items.prompt: What about costs that don't belong to anyone, like public gateways?
items.answer: Shared costs are divided according to separate distribution rules. Disputes can be reduced if rules such as usage ratio and equal division are agreed upon in advance. The rules are written down so that anyone can check them.

items.prompt: What are attribution rules used for?
items.answer: It becomes a common basis for expense reporting, showbacks and chargebacks, and limit setting. Once a decision is made well, it can be reused in many places, so the initial design is important. If the same attribution unit is used as the standard for setting limits, reporting and control will not be inconsistent.

screens.outro: Now that we've established the need for attribution, let's gather the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Expand items to see evidence
screens.lead: When you select each item, the basis for the summary statement will unfold. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.title: The cost is the amount of usage for each token type multiplied by the unit price, so you must know how to read the price list structure.
items.body: Input, output, cache read, and cache write each have a unit cost, and multipliers such as area or fast mode are accumulated. Since the unit cost of output is usually higher, it is important which token increases. You need to be able to read structures, not numbers, to respond to the new price list.

items.title: The Usage & Cost API divides usage by model, key, and workspace and compares it with billing.
items.body: Group by days, hours, and minutes and divide by group_by. SDK's total_cost_usd is an estimate and is not used for confirmation. Use this API when you need accurate token counting and billing matching.

items.title: Workspace and FinOps allocations attribute costs to teams and projects
items.body: Place keys and limits on your workspace and determine who is responsible for the three pillars of allocation, tagging, and shared costs. Both showback and chargeback are possible only if there is an allocation. If you need per-user limits like Claude Code, configure a separate workspace.

items.title: In shared resources, measurement and attribution are designed directly and proprietary information is provided at the time of creation.
items.body: Since shared services often do not automatically classify usage by tenant, representative indicators are determined and measured directly. Ownership information is enforced when creating a resource. You've already accumulated unclaimed costs to fill it up later.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's think about it in relation to our own work.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms in this class are token charging, price list, Usage & Cost API, and workspace-specific costs. Let's go back to the original question. What information is needed first on a bill that only shows the total?

It's the pieces that add up: which model, which day, which token type was used, and which team's share. If you can break down your usage into these units, the numbers on your bill will explain. Conversely, if it cannot be divided, changing the structure first is a priority rather than reducing costs.

Check your organization's current structure. You can check whether one key is being used in multiple places, whether development and operations are in the same bundle, and find the cause of increased costs within minutes.

If changing the structure is difficult, start by enforcing ownership information at the time of resource creation. Setting up just one naming convention or tag will make subsequent attribution much easier. And remember the rule that costs are always determined by claims data, not estimates. Just following these two things, enforcing ownership information and confirming billing data, will make cost accounting much easier.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: At what point does my job get stuck regarding token charging? Now, think about what services in your organization have the most cost uncertainty, and whether you can break down the costs of those services by model and team.

checks.q: In the month-end bill, the number of input tokens was similar to last month, but the amount increased as the output tokens increased significantly. What best explains this?
options: Input and output have the same unit cost, so if the total tokens increase, the cost increases at the same rate.
There is no unit price attached to the output token, only the input token is charged.
The unit price of output tokens is usually higher than that of input, so as output increases, the cost increases significantly even with the same increase in tokens.
The cost rose because the cache read unit price was higher than the input unit price.
checks.explain: Cost is the sum of input and output multiplied by their respective unit costs, and the output unit price is generally higher than the input. Cached input is calculated as a separate read cost.

wrong.0: The unit costs of input and output are calculated differently.
wrong.1: There is also a unit price attached to the output token.
wrong.3: The cache read unit price is generally set lower than the general input unit price.

checks.intro: This is a case where the input token is similar but the billing amount has increased. Find out the cause.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Output tokens usually have a higher unit price than inputs, so as output increases, the cost rises more significantly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Input and output have different unit prices and are charged for both. Remember that cost is the sum of each unit price multiplied by each unit.

checks.q: Match the following terms and descriptions
right: Actual billing of costs to those responsible
This is an estimate calculated from local price lists and may differ from actual charges.
API to programmatically query an organization's past usage and costs and compare them with billing
Just showing the costs to those responsible.
checks.explain: The Usage and Cost API is used for accurate counting and billing comparison, and the SDK estimates are not used as a basis for confirmation. Both showback and chargeback are possible only when there is an allocation of costs to those responsible.
checks.intro: Match the terms used in cost counting with explanations.
checks.correctFeedback: All are correct. You made a distinction between billing comparison APIs and estimates, showbacks that only show you, and chargebacks that actually bill you.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatched pair. Check the difference in the Usage and Cost API for accurate tallies, total_cost_usd is an estimate, Showback is only disclosed, and Chargeback is actually charged.

checks.q: When your expenses increase this month, try putting them in order to track them back to the cause.
items: Use the Usage API to group usage by day and model to find where the increase has occurred.
Input, output, and cache tokens are multiplied by each unit price and compared with the billing.
Divide into workspaces to check for growth in specific projects.
Take action on the cause and confirm it with claims data, not estimates.
checks.explain: Start with a broad scope and gradually narrow it down to find the cause. Confirmation is based on billing data, not SDK estimates.
checks.intro: Try to sequence the causes of cost increases from broad to narrow.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. You have set the flow for confirmation with usage grouping, unit price comparison, confirmation by workspace, and billing data.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is out of order. You need to first find where the growth is, gradually narrow it down, and finally confirm it with billing data, not SDK estimates.

glossary.def: This method calculates the cost by multiplying the number of input and output tokens by each unit price. Cache reads and writes incur separate unit costs.
This table contains input, output, cash unit price and discount for each model, and multipliers according to region and speed.
This is an Admin API that searches an organization's past usage and costs by dividing them into models, workspaces, keys, etc.
It is a structure that divides usage by dividing keys and limits on a project or team basis.

This is the FinOps Framework's ability to allocate costs to each responsible person through metadata such as accounts, tags, and labels. It consists of allocation, tagging and tiering, and shared cost strategies.

This is a perspective that divides the responsibility for the measurement provided by the platform and the responsibility for attribution and control that must be carried out directly by the customer.

misconceptions.myth: The cost informed by the SDK is the billing amount.
misconceptions.fact: total_cost_usd is an estimate calculated from local price lists and may differ from your actual charge. Confirmation is based on billing data.

misconceptions.myth: The output and input unit costs are the same.
misconceptions.fact: In general, the output cost is higher, and the cache has separate unit costs for reads and writes.
Costs are lumped together and teams cannot be held accountable. Workspaces or keys must be divided so that they can be attributed.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The cost is the amount of usage for each token type multiplied by the unit price, so you must know how to read the price list structure.
Use the Usage & Cost API to match your billing by dividing your usage by model, key, and workspace.
Workspace and FinOps allocations attribute costs to teams and projects.
In shared resources, metering and attribution are designed directly and proprietary information is provided at the time of resource creation.
